1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bg.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain and aims it at the knight that defends d5 and guards e4: trading it would loosen Black's grip on the centre. White builds pressure on d5 while Black prepares a freeing break, the slow strategic game typical of this opening.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bg.name: Queen's Gambit Declined

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bf.strategy: Keeps the bishop outside the pawn chain, on the diagonal towards c7 and e5, and makes the knight exchanges that ease Black's game against a bishop on g5 less effective. It is a quieter, more manoeuvring way to fight for the centre, with more pieces kept on.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bf.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Harrwitz Attack
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bf.background: Peter Leko, usually a player of 1.e4, used it with White to beat Vladimir Kramnik in their 2004 World Championship match. Bobby Fischer played the line in game 14 of his 1972 match against Boris Spassky.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.e3.strategy: A solid, modest move that supports d4 and frees the king's bishop, but it shuts the queen's bishop in behind the pawn chain, the piece that usually needs a good square in this opening. White is safe and flexible, but Black has an easy game.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bf.strategy: Castles and puts the king out of the centre. Nothing is threatened, since the queen guards c7, so Black can ignore the bishop and complete development. The king is safe and the rook comes towards the centre, ready for a freeing pawn break.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bg.strategy: Gets the king to safety and a rook towards the centre. The knight on f6 is shielded by the bishop on e7, so the bishop on g5 threatens nothing yet. Black keeps the solid structure and waits for White to show how the pressure will grow.

Asks the bishop at once what it intends. If White trades on f6, Black recaptures with the bishop and has the two bishops; if the bishop retreats, Black has put the question for free and the pawn on h6 gives the king some room.

Supports d5 solidly, but leaves the king in the centre and the light-squared bishop shut in, while the bishop on g5 stays aimed at the knight on f6. It is playable but slow, and it gives White time to finish development.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.e3.strategy: Castles before White has shown a plan. The king is safe and the rook comes towards the centre, so Black can wait. The standing worry is the c8-bishop shut in behind e6, freed later by a ...c5 break or by taking on c4 once White's bishop has committed itself.
